bio.en: Tim Holley is VP of Product at Etsy, where over 10+ years he helped grow GMV from around $500 million to over $13 billion.
bio.zh: Tim Holley 是 Etsy 的产品副总裁，在逾十年的时间里，他帮助该公司将 GMV（成交额）从约 5 亿美元增长到超过 130 亿美元。

summary.en: Tim shares the big cultural transition Etsy went through as it scaled, and the product and marketplace moves that drove its growth from $500M to $13B+ in GMV. He discusses how to change internal culture, where to find leverage in a two-sided marketplace, and advice for anyone working on marketplaces or seeking growth ideas. The episode is a rare inside look at scaling one of the world's most distinctive marketplaces.
summary.zh: Tim 分享了 Etsy 在规模化过程中经历的重大文化转型，以及推动其 GMV 从 5 亿增长到 130 多亿美元的产品与市场动作。他讨论了如何改变内部文化、在双边市场中何处寻找杠杆，以及给所有做市场平台或寻求增长思路之人的建议。本期是对规模化全球最具特色市场平台之一的罕见内部透视。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: When the CDC mandated face masks in early April 2020, that's when essentially we went to sleep one day with our typical April traffic, typical April sales, and then it was Black Friday overnight. And in part, because nobody knew where to find face masks. Our sellers are incredibly astute business people. And if you had been making wedding dresses, and you know how to sew, and you've got material, and you've got a bit of time, making a mask is quite a simple task. And so we just saw this huge surge of demand, and then supply rising to meet it. (00:00:37): And we did something that as far as I know, we've never done in Etsy's past, which is we put out a call to our sellers to say, "Now's the time. Now's the time to make face masks if you can." And so it felt like this is our time to shine, to really help sellers continue to make sales, to help buyers find this critical item that they were looking for. (00:00:57): And then from there, things kept going, and we really worked hard to make sure that the story was not just about face masks for our buyers, that they understood that Etsy's a place for so many different categories and so many different items.
turns.zh:
2020年4月初，当美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）强制要求佩戴口罩时，我们一觉醒来便面临着完全不同的局面——四月的交通繁忙、销售活跃，转眼间就迎来了“黑色星期五”促销狂欢。究其原因，关键在于当时人们根本找不到口罩货源。我们的卖家们都是精明的商人——如果你擅长缝纫，手头有面料，再加上一点时间制作口罩其实并不难。于是我们见证了需求激增，供应也随之跟上节奏。（00:00:37）  
我们做了一件据我所知Etsy历史上从未有过的事——向卖家们发出紧急呼吁：“现在是行动的时候了！如果你们能做到，就赶紧生产口罩吧。”那一刻，我们感觉到了自己的价值所在——帮助卖家继续开展销售，为买家找到他们急需的关键防护产品。（00:00:57）  
此后，一切顺势而为。我们竭尽全力向买家传递这样的信息：Etsy不仅仅是销售口罩的平台，这里还汇聚着无数品类、海量商品，满足人们的多样化需求。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Thank you for having me on, Lenny, really appreciate it. Looking forward to it.
turns.zh: 伦尼，感谢你邀请我，真的很感激。期待今天的交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm looking forward to it even more. So you've been at Etsy for I think over 10 years, although I did notice that you left for a year and ended up leading product at SoulCycle. So first of all, what is that about? What happened there?
turns.zh: 我期待得更迫切了。你加入Etsy已经超过10年了吧？不过我注意到你曾离开一年，在SoulCycle担任产品负责人。首先，能讲讲那段经历吗？当时发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, at the time, I'd been at Etsy for over six years, and I just had the itch. I wanted to go work on a different product, build different things, experience different industry. Along, had a theory that working on the proactive side of healthcare, meaning fitness and wellness, is how you achieve better outcomes. And it felt like SoulCycle was a really interesting way to do that. Pretty well-known brand, high street presence in many cities. Could you affect change through that? (00:05:12): Ultimately realized it wasn't a place that I wanted to spend a ton of time and energy. And so through a lot of soul-searching, grown, I know I found my way back to Etsy, really anchoring on three things. One, working on a product that you care about that adds value to other people's lives. And so what we do every day at Etsy is we help our sellers make sales, and that's really meaningful for the vast majority of them. It's reaching an audience that they wouldn't be able to reach. And so that feels like a really great thing to get up every morning and work on. (00:05:46): And so that's maybe the business and the product side, and the other side is people. It might sound a little twee, but just working with people who you can learn from and who you respect, and ultimately can have fun working with, it matters a ton. We spend a lot of time of our days and our lives at work, and so doing it with people who you really value, it's awesome. (00:06:05): I have one memory that we used to have an engineer who used to be a standup comedian, and so that really pushed the boundaries of what a standup meant every day. And it was always a little fun, a little exciting. You never quite knew what you were going to get. And so just little things like that, they make the work life really, really great.
turns.zh: 是的，当时我在Etsy待了六年多，突然心血来潮，想尝试不同产品，开发新领域，探索不同行业。我坚信，主动参与医疗健康领域（比如健身和健康管理）能带来更好的成果。SoulCycle是个很有趣的切入点——它是知名品牌，在很多城市都有实体门店。能通过这样的平台推动变革吗？（00:05:12）但后来发现那份工作并不值得投入太多精力。经过深思熟虑，我回归了Etsy，主要基于三个核心：一是参与自己热爱、能为他人创造价值的产品。在Etsy，我们每天帮助卖家提升销售业绩，这对绝大多数卖家意义重大——让他们能触达更广泛的客户群体。这份工作让我每天充满热情。（00:05:46）其次是团队。说起来可能有点俗气，但与能相互学习、相互尊重、共事愉快的伙伴共事至关重要。我们大部分时间都在工作场所度过，能与真心敬重的人共事真是太棒了。（00:06:05）我记得我们曾有一位工程师曾是单口喜剧演员，他每天都突破单口喜剧的界限。工作氛围总是充满趣味和惊喜，你永远不知道会发生什么。正是这些小细节，让工作生活变得格外美好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's hilarious. I never thought it that way. I feel like every standup needs a standup comedian in their standup. Sounds like that should be part of agile. We should need to change the manifesto. (00:06:35): So I've always seen the Etsy journey from the outside, and so there's a few things that I've always wanted to dig into. One is I just remember this New York Times story back in the day when your current CEO Josh Silverman joined, and it felt like a huge moment in the history of Etsy, where it feels like it just kind of transitioned from this touchy feely, everyone loves each other moment to just like, "Hey guys, we got to build a real business here that's sustainable." And it feels like many startups have to go through that transition where it's like, "Nothing's ever going to change. It's going to be so we're all family here," to just, "Things have to change. This isn't working." I'm curious what that was like living through that.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。我从未这么想过。我觉得每个单口喜剧演员的团队里都应该有单口喜剧演员。这听起来应该成为敏捷开发的一部分。我们应该修改敏捷宣言。（00:06:35）我一直从外部观察Etsy的历程，有几个问题一直想深入探讨。首先，我记得当年你现任CEO乔希·西尔弗曼加入时，《纽约时报》做了报道，感觉那是Etsy历史上的重要时刻，标志着公司从温馨友好的“大家庭”模式转向“必须建立可持续商业模式”的严肃阶段。很多初创公司都经历过这种转变，从“永远不变，我们都是一家亲”到“必须变革，否则不行”。我很好奇你如何度过这个过程。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, I mean the first thing I'll say is it was a hard transition, and I was personally fortunate in the sense that the transition you're speaking of in 2017 also happened to coincide with rounds of layoffs. And I was super fortunate that I didn't lose my job, so I don't want to presuppose that my version of hard is the same as another person's version of hard. (00:07:38): But I think a lot of us, and myself included, we had a lot of our identity tied up in Etsy and what we're doing, a really deep passion for the mission of the business and what we're trying to achieve. I just mentioned helping small independent sellers. And just to be clear, that hasn't gone away. I think that that's something we've been really successful at pulling through as a line that was true 10 years ago and is still true today. But it was a time when we were really forced to rethink a lot of how we worked and what we worked on. (00:08:12): Just to use a small example, we had had a pretty entrenched consensus-based culture, where we would really debate a lot of decisions and a lot of features. And on the one hand, I think that that does lead to good outcomes, right? Thoughtful products that have a lot of viewpoints really baked into the core of the thinking. (00:08:33): On the other hand, not fast. When you have your identity tied up in the company and what you do, and then you're kind of being asked or you realize that you need to change how you're working, it can feel pretty existential. It's really cutting to the core of who you are and things that you hold really true. (00:08:53): The reality is it's a business, and we needed to get faster at launching features, improving the experience, and ultimately, having a predictable way to drive GMS, gross merchandise sales, which is our north star KPI. And so it definitely took some time to work through that, but we got to a good place, and the results over the last few years to some degree speak for themselves. But it was a testing and trying time for sure.
turns.zh: 是的，我首先想说的是，这个转变确实很艰难。就我个人而言，幸运的是，你所提到的2017年那次转型恰好与一轮轮裁员同时发生。我很庆幸自己没有失业，所以我不想预先假定我所经历的困难就等同于其他人的经历。（00:07:38）但我认为，我们很多人——包括我在内——都将自己的身份与Etsy以及我们正在做的事情紧密联系在一起，对公司的使命和我们努力实现的目标怀有深深的热情。我刚刚提到的帮助小型独立卖家的工作。但要明确的是，这份热情从未消退。我认为，这是我们成功延续下来的传统——十年前如此，至今依然如此。但那段时期确实迫使我们重新审视很多工作方式和研发方向。（00:08:12）举个小例子，我们曾深深扎根于共识文化中，对许多决策和功能都会展开激烈讨论。一方面，我认为这种文化确实能带来好的结果——经过深思熟虑的产品往往能将多种观点融入核心思维。（00:08:33）但另一方面，这种方式效率不高。当你将自己的身份与公司及工作紧密相连时，被要求或意识到需要改变工作方式时，那种感觉会很深刻。这真的触及了你的核心价值观和坚守的信念。（00:08:53）现实是，这是一家企业，我们需要更快地推出新功能、提升用户体验，最终找到可预测的方式来推动GMS（毛商品销售额）——这是我们的核心KPI。当然，这确实需要时间来克服，但我们最终找到了正确的方向，过去几年的成果在一定程度上说明了一切。不过那确实是一段充满考验和探索的时期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm always curious how these changes play out and what works in making change. Is there something that you remember that Josh did well or that leaders did well to help that transition?
turns.zh: 我一直很好奇这些变革是如何展开的，以及哪些做法有助于推动变革。你是否记得乔希在帮助完成这次转变时做得好的地方，或者其他领导者做得好的方面？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: One thing that is just such a standout is having... And I mentioned GMS as our north star KPI, just having that, being absolutely front and center, being the drumbeat that we talk about in every meeting, the measuring stick that we measure the success of launches against. And maybe it's a bit surprising, but we didn't have that type of clarity in the past. (00:09:51): And so rallying everyone around that. And you might not pay into it directly. You might pay into it through one or two levels of abstraction, but you're still clearly aligned with what the company's trying to achieve. And that was something that was a really stark difference, and I think that helped. (00:10:09): It helped the prioritization discussion a lot. If you can't really articulate why this thing matters to driving GMS and the type of timeframe that we're talking about, be it a quarter or 12 months out, and different projects will contribute in different ways. But that was just one huge standout, and that's been a drumbeat over the years that let's continue to stay focused on that as a metric. (00:10:32): The other thing to me is bringing an outside in perspective, really benchmarking against your competitors and your competitive set. Don't get me wrong, I think Etsy is a unique marketplace. Our sellers are independent sellers. They sell unique items. The reality though is that our buyers are shopping all over the internet. They're shopping on High Street, they're shopping in different places. And so we have to be aware of the broader context of where they're spending their dollars helps us make better decisions over time. (00:11:04): And so on the one hand, there is no one-to-one direct competitor to Etsy. But there are other businesses and other brands that are competing for eyeballs or wallets that we need to be aware of. And bringing that into the discussion was a really helpful one that helped ground us in the overall dynamics of what buyers are doing,, where they're spending their money, and how they think about us.
turns.zh:
有一件非常突出的事情，那就是……我提到了GMS是我们的北极星KPI指标，始终将其置于核心位置，在每次会议中反复强调，以此作为衡量新品发布成功与否的标尺。说实话，过去我们并没有这种清晰的定位。（00:09:51）所以，我们需要让所有人围绕这个目标团结起来。即使你不直接参与其中，也可能通过一两层抽象的层级来参与，但你始终与公司的战略目标保持清晰的对齐。这是巨大的转变，我认为这对我们帮助很大。
（00:10:09）这极大地推动了优先级讨论的进程。如果你无法清晰阐述某项工作对推动GMS的重要性，以及我们所谈论的时间框架——无论是季度还是12个月——不同项目将以不同方式做出贡献，那么这就是一个关键的突破点。这几年来，这个理念始终在推动我们将GMS作为核心指标持续聚焦。
（00:10:32）另一件让我印象深刻的事，是引入外部视角，真正与竞争对手和同行进行对标。别误会，我认为Etsy是一个独特的市场平台。我们的卖家是独立卖家，他们销售独特商品。但现实是，买家在互联网上四处购物。他们在High Street（知名购物平台）购物，在不同平台购物。因此，我们必须了解他们把钱花在哪里的更广泛背景，这有助于我们随着时间推移做出更明智的决策。
（00:11:04）所以，Etsy没有直接的竞争对手。但有其他企业和品牌在争夺用户注意力或消费份额，我们需要对此保持警惕。将这些因素纳入讨论非常有益，它帮助我们理解买家的行为模式、消费偏好，以及他们对我们的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you took away as a leader from watching that shift, that you bring to making change, transitioning people to working in a different way?
turns.zh: 作为领导者，在观察到这种转变后，你还获得了哪些启发，并将其应用于推动变革、引导团队以不同方式工作？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Definitely focus on a clear KPI that the teams can rally around. That's one. The other is... And I respect Josh immensely on his ability to tell a really clear narrative and use that consistently over time. The old adage of you need to say something three times before people understand it. I would wager you need to say it another three times before they internalize it. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And having that be part of the day-to-day conversation, it seems like such a small thing, but it adds up to having clarity on goal, the KPI point, and then clarity on why, the narrative point. If you can marry those two things, I think that's an incredibly powerful combination.
turns.zh: 绝对要专注于一个团队可以团结在周围的清晰KPI。这是第一点。另外，我非常敬重Josh，他能够清晰地讲述一个故事，并持续保持一致性。俗话说，你需要把一件事说三遍，人们才会理解。我敢打赌，你需要再说三遍，他们才会真正内化。[新段落]将这件事纳入日常对话，看似微不足道，但它有助于我们对目标、KPI要点，以及背后的原因——即叙事要点——保持清晰。如果你能将这两者结合起来，我认为这是一个极其强大的组合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While we're on this topic, I'm curious what Etsy's values are. I imagine you've codified a few, we call them core values at are Airbnbs or something like that at Etsy. And if so, I'm curious what they are.
turns.zh: 既然我们谈到这个话题，我很好奇Etsy的价值观是什么。我想你们已经将其正式化，我们称之为核心价值观，就像Airbnb或其他公司那样。那么，请问它们具体是什么呢？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: We call them guiding principles at Etsy. We have a few of them, and I won't go through all of them, but just to give you a flavor, one of them is around digging deeper, and that really speaks to aiming to really understand the why behind a change, to really push on the insights that we're learning through qual or quant research, or other inputs that we might be looking at in order to make the best decision possible with the information we have at the time. (00:12:52): Another example of a principle is minimizing waste. It aligns with how we think about product development, which is, we want to know, is the work we're doing adding value to the customer and the business? And so something that isn't working out a lot of times in product development we're wrong. And so being able to say, "No, this is no longer valuable, we need to move on to the next thing," has been something that's served us really well. (00:13:17): Ultimately, we are quite a small team. There's just over 2,000 people in the business, and if you then scale back to engineering and product, we're not big. And so we have to be really diligent about how we're investing our time and our resources in order to be successful.
turns.zh: 在Etsy，我们将这些理念称为指导原则。我们有几条这样的原则，我就不一一详述了。但就让您领略一下其中一条：深入挖掘。这意味着要努力理解变革背后的深层原因，深入挖掘我们通过定性或定量研究、或其他数据输入所获得的洞察，从而在当时掌握的信息基础上做出最明智的决策。（00:12:52）：另一个原则例子是减少浪费。这与我们的产品开发理念高度契合——我们需要审视所做的工作是否为客户和业务创造了价值。在产品开发过程中，如果某项工作效果不佳，我们通常会承认错误。能够果断地说“不，这项工作已无价值，我们需要转向下一个方向”，对我们来说非常有效。（00:13:17）：归根结底，我们是一个规模不大的团队。整个公司仅有2000多名员工，如果再缩小到工程和产品团队，我们的规模就更小了。因此，我们必须非常审慎地分配时间和资源，才能确保业务成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so another big moment as an outsider that it feels like Etsy went through is during Covid. There's this huge transition to e-commerce, and I think Etsy was a big beneficiary of that. People wanting to buy more stuff online, go to stores less. And it feels like it was a huge accelerant for the business. I'm curious just what that experience was like leading the product team through that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，作为局外人，我觉得Etsy经历过的一个重大转折点是在新冠疫情期间。当时电商迎来巨大变革，Etsy显然从中受益匪浅。人们更倾向于在线购物，减少实体店消费。这对Etsy的业务无疑是一个巨大的增长引擎。我很好奇，在带领产品团队度过这段时期时，您有怎样的经历？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: It was quite wild, I'll say that. And to be more specific, as many or all of us did in probably the world of tech at least, we went home not knowing what the next weeks or weeks as we thought would bring, turns out years. But when the CDC mandated face masks in, I think it was early April 2020, that's when essentially we went to sleep one day with our typical April traffic, typical April sales, and then it was Black Friday overnight. (00:14:26): And in part because nobody knew where to find face masks. Our sellers are incredibly astute business people. And if you had been making wedding dresses, and you know how to sew, and you've got material, and you've got a bit of time, making a mask is quite a simple task. And so we just saw this huge surge of demand, and then supply rising to meet it. (00:14:47): And we did something that far as I know we've never done an Etsy's past, which is we put out a call to our sellers to say, "Now's the time. Now's the time to make face masks if you can." And so it felt like this is our time to shine, to really help sellers continue to make sales, to help buyers find this critical item that they were looking for. (00:15:08): So it was a very, very exciting couple of weeks while we were kind of adapting to that change. And we were just really... Every day there would be standups. "What's happening? What do we need to change?" (00:15:20): I remember distinctly, we were worried about certain sellers not being able to meet the demand that they were seeing. And so we did the old-fashioned thing, of not personally, but we called them and we said, "How are you guys doing? What can we do to help?" And some people said, "We've got this, don't worry. This is squarely in our wheelhouse. We can absolutely meet the supply." And others said, "Actually, we need a little bit of help. We need to take a pause for a moment while we catch up with all these orders, and then we can come back to taking more." [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And so just getting back to good old-fashioned know your customer, what do they need from you at that moment was just a really kind of powerful thing that took away from that time. (00:16:03): And then from there, things kept going, and we really worked hard to make sure that the story was not just about face masks for our buyers, that they understood that Etsy's a place for so many different categories and so many different items. And that was then the next phase of the challenge. We got a huge influx of new or reactivated buyers. How do we keep them around? How do we make sure that the product does a little bit more work to retain them, and can really have hooks that bring them back time and again? And so that was kind of the journey that we then went on mid-2020, to probably the subsequent 18 months or so.
turns.zh: 当时情况相当混乱，我得这么说。更具体地说，我们中许多人——至少在科技领域——回家后都不知道未来几周甚至几年会发生什么。但当美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）于2020年4月初强制要求佩戴口罩时，那一天我们仿佛从正常的四月交通和销售状况中醒来，转眼间就迎来了“黑色星期五”般的销售狂潮。（00:14:26）部分原因是当时没人知道去哪儿能买到口罩。我们的卖家都是精明的商人。比如，如果你原本在制作婚纱，擅长缝纫，有面料和空闲时间，那么制作口罩就是件简单的事。因此，我们见证了需求的激增，随后供应也迅速跟上来。（00:14:47）据我所知，这是Etsy史无前例的举措——我们向卖家发出号召：“现在是行动的时候了。如果你们能做到，就赶紧生产口罩吧。” 那段时间，我们仿佛迎来了一个大放异彩的机遇，既能帮助卖家继续销售，又能满足买家对关键防护产品的需求。（00:15:08）在适应新变化的过程中，那真是令人兴奋的几周。每天我们都会开例会：“情况如何？我们需要做出哪些调整？” （00:15:20）我清楚地记得，当时我们担心某些卖家无法满足激增的需求。于是我们采取了传统做法——虽然没有亲自联系，但还是打电话询问：“你们情况如何？我们能如何提供帮助？” 有些卖家说：“别担心，这完全在我们的能力范围内。我们能满足供应需求。” 另一些则说：“实际上，我们需要暂停一下，先处理完这些订单，再考虑增加产量。” 回到“了解客户需求”的基本要点，这正是那段时期最有力的法宝。（00:16:03）此后，我们持续努力，确保买家对Etsy的认知不止于口罩，而是认识到这里汇聚着众多品类和商品。这便成为接下来挑战的核心任务。大量新用户和回流用户涌入平台，我们如何留住他们？如何让产品设计更具吸引力，反复吸引他们回访？这便是2020年中至随后约18个月间我们的探索之旅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you learned as a leader working in leading teams through that time? It must've been a pretty surreal experience, a lot of stress, people worrying about their own health.
turns.zh: 在那段时期，作为领导者带领团队应对挑战，你学到了什么？那一定是一段相当超现实的经历，压力巨大，人们都为自身健康担忧。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I was one of the fortunate ones back then. No kids, worked in an industry that was clearly critical at the time. So I am in awe of how parents worked through that time. So stressful yes, but not to the extent that other people experienced the stress of Covid. (00:17:05): We just tried a lot of stuff. I remember early on, I think we had maybe even daily, but at least three times a week coffee chats with the team, just like, "How are you guys doing? What's going on?" And at a certain point we realized all we're talking about is exactly the same things. Nobody wants to be on more calls and more video video chats. And so we just continued to evolve, and really try to keep a pulse on what the team needs. (00:17:29): And that, like I said, given context of being parents or whatever, differed pretty dramatically person to person. So definitely wasn't a one size fits all solution. That's more on the people side. (00:17:40): I think on the product side, as I mentioned, we were really starting to get focused on driving retention, or maybe said slightly differently, driving frequency. And that was a newer topic for us. We've long at Etsy been a really, and maybe rose-tinted glasses speaking a little bit, but a really great experiment, A/B testing driven culture. And so when you think about things like retention, you can absolutely test, course I'm not saying you can't, but you're looking at a different time horizon. Instead of someone making a purchase in that visit or in a week, you're looking at do they come back in 30 days, in 60 days, in 90 days? (00:18:19): And so that forced us out of our comfort zone to some degree in terms of how we understand, how we measure change, how long we're willing to wait to see it show up. Back to the incrementality point on minimizing waste, is this actually adding value to the business? And so those were great challenges to tackle, of course on a pretty heightened degree of intensity and focus from the business. But that was an exciting time.
turns.zh: 当时我算幸运儿之一，没有孩子，所在的行业在当时显然至关重要。所以我对那些在那段时期带孩子的父母们深感敬佩。压力确实很大，但远不及新冠疫情期间人们所承受的压力程度。（00:17:05）：我们尝试了很多方法。我记得早期阶段，我们可能每周都开三次团队咖啡会——“大家最近怎么样？有什么新动态？”但到某个阶段，我们意识到大家讨论的内容几乎千篇一律。没人想参加更多电话会议和视频聊天。所以我们不断调整，努力掌握团队的真实需求。（00:17:29）：正如我所说，在父母身份或其他情况下，每个人的应对方式差异巨大。所以这绝不是一刀切的解决方案。这更多涉及人员管理层面。（00:17:40）：在产品层面，如我所说，我们开始专注于提升用户留存率，或者更准确地说，提升用户活跃频率。这对我们来说是个新课题。在Etsy，我们长期秉持着以A/B测试为驱动的文化理念，尽管可能有些理想化。但当考虑留存率时，我们可以进行测试——当然不是说不能测试，但测试的时间维度不同。不是关注用户在访问或一周内完成购买，而是观察他们在30天、60天、90天内的回访频率。（00:18:19）：这在某种程度上迫使我们跳出舒适区，重新审视如何理解和衡量变化，如何耐心等待数据反馈。回到增量思维，如何最大化资源利用，创造商业价值？当然，公司对此高度重视，赋予了高度的关注度。但那段时光确实令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So speaking of that, I want to chat about the marketplace and the marketplace you've built and things you've learned from building. I think it's one of the, I don't know, maybe top 10 marketplace businesses in the world, somewhere in there. And first of all, I'm curious just broadly, what have you learned is really important to just building a really successful thriving marketplace? And then I'll dig into more details. But just broadly, is there anything that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 好的。说到这，我想聊聊你们打造的这个市场平台，以及从中获得的经验教训。我认为它可能是全球十大市场平台之一，或者说在某个排名里能跻身前列。首先，我很好奇，打造一个真正成功、蓬勃发展的市场平台，有哪些关键要素？接下来我会深入探讨具体细节，但先从宏观层面入手，有什么值得借鉴的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: This narrative is still there, but I think we really focused heavily on the seller side, so the supply side of the business early on. And we really immersed ourselves in who sellers are, what they need, and how what they need maybe differs from what the solutions that they can find elsewhere. (00:19:30): Back in the day, we were doing studio visits with sellers. We were going to their workshops, we were going to their homes. We were seeing how they make items, we were seeing how they package and ship them out. We were bringing them into the office when we were running hack weeks to say, "Hey, we've got this crazy idea. Is this interesting?" So trying to involve them in the product development process to the extent that it was reasonable or feasible. (00:19:57): And so I think that served us really well. We have a very deep and rich understanding of our sellers. And then the next phase and the more recent phase has been, how do we create a world-class buyer experience that ultimately drives sales for our sellers? Because when you have over 100 million items, all of which are unique, you've got a different challenge than when you have 10,000 SKUs that you could kind of find anywhere or on many retailers. (00:20:22): And so topics like structured data, topics like how do we help you gain confidence? Buyer this thing will meet your needs from a seller who you may never have heard of. They don't have a brand that you you've ever encountered before. And so we have some kind of somewhat unique challenges on that front where we need to lean into themes that other marketplaces absolutely touch on. (00:20:45): For example, customer reviews play a big role in our experience, but they play a heightened role given the things I mentioned, right? Unique inventory from a seller that is maybe an independent person who is a single entrepreneur, it's one person.
turns.zh: 这种叙事模式至今依然存在，但我认为我们最初确实非常关注卖家端，也就是业务的供应侧。我们深入研究了卖家是谁、他们的需求是什么，以及他们的需求与其他平台能提供的解决方案有何不同。（00:19:30）：回想当年，我们会去卖家的工作室、家中拜访，观察他们如何制作商品、如何包装和发货。在举办黑客周活动时，我们会把他们带到办公室，说：“嘿，我们有个疯狂的想法，你觉得有意思吗？”尽可能让他们参与产品开发过程。（00:19:57）：这对我们帮助很大。我们对卖家有了深刻而全面的理解。接下来阶段，也就是最近阶段，我们的重点转向如何打造世界级的买家体验，最终推动卖家销售增长。因为当平台上有超过1亿件商品，且每件商品都独一无二时，面临的挑战与拥有1万种SKU、且这些SKU在其他零售平台随处可得的情况截然不同。（00:20:22）：比如结构化数据，比如如何帮助买家建立信任？当买家面对一个可能从未听说过、没有品牌背书的卖家时，他们会担忧商品能否满足需求。在这方面，我们需要应对其他市场平台早已应对过的挑战。（00:20:45）：例如，客户评价在我们的平台上发挥着重要作用，但在上述背景下，其重要性被进一步放大。毕竟，卖家可能是个独立创业者，他们的独特库存对买家而言更具吸引力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you mentioned that initially, the focus was on sellers, which is really interesting because a lot of marketplaces, first of all need to figure out which side do we focus on? Who do we cater to most? And the way you described it is initially it was how do we make sure the sellers that are joining at Etsy are most well-served? And then later on it became more of a focus on the buyer side?
turns.zh: 你提到最初重点放在卖家身上，这真的很有趣，因为很多市场平台首先需要确定专注哪一方？谁是主要服务对象？你描述的情况是，最初如何确保加入Etsy的卖家得到最好的服务？后来重点转向买家端？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, I guess I'm painting it as a linear approach. It certainly was not. Because if you've got supply without demand, then you don't really have a marketplace. If you've got demand and no supply to meet it, then you also don't have a marketplace. So there's this flip-flop between, do you have enough supply to satiate the demand you have? And playing that out is certainly, I feel like art, not necessarily strictly science.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得我把这描绘成一个线性过程，但实际上并非如此。因为如果只有供应没有需求，那么就没有市场了。如果只有需求而没有供应来满足需求，那同样没有市场。所以在两者之间摇摆——你是否有足够的供应来满足现有需求？把这件事玩转，确实像是一门艺术，而非严格的科学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I'm curious how you all think about that actually. So at Airbnb, there's always this thinking of, who do we prioritize if we have to make a decision? is it host or guest? And it's shifted over the years at Airbnb. How do you all think about that as a, "Here's who we're going to prioritize if we really have to make a decision"?
turns.zh: 是的。所以我很好奇你们大家对此有何看法。在Airbnb，总是会思考，如果必须做出决定，我们优先考虑哪一方？是房东还是房客？Airbnb多年来也在这个问题上不断调整。你们如何看待“如果必须做出决定，我们将优先考虑哪一方”这个问题？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: And maybe to your point, that's also evolved at Etsy. And the place we're in at the moment is the job of a marketplace, even pre the technology definition of a marketplace is a seller will go there to make sales. And if they're not making sales, they probably won't go to that marketplace. And so we really see it as paramount that we have a qualified set of buyers who are looking for the items, the type of items our sellers are selling, and that we can help them make a purchase decision, and therefore a seller maker sale. (00:22:41): That doesn't mean that every single team is working on building features for buyers because it doesn't work. Not least because you have a limited piece of real estate marketplace. And if you have too many teams working on it at one time, you'll end up getting in each other's way, and you won't be that productive. And so of course, we have a team that's laser focused on improving the seller experience. How do they list their inventory? How do they manage their sales? How do they fulfill their items? As one example. (00:23:08): But really back to the GMS is the north star, GMS represents a buyer buying from a seller. So it doesn't necessarily say build only for one of your audiences or one of your customers, but it says that that's really the job to be done here is helping facilitate that transaction.
turns.zh: 或许正如你所言，Etsy也经历了类似的演变。当前我们的定位是市场平台，即便在技术层面对市场平台的定义是，卖家会去那里销售商品。如果他们销售不出去，通常就不会再去那个平台。因此，我们认为最重要的是，要有优质的买家群体，他们正在寻找与卖家所售商品类型相契合的商品，并且我们要帮助他们做出购买决策，从而促成卖家与买家的交易。（00:22:41）：这并不意味着每个团队都在致力于为买家开发功能，因为这行不通。尤其是因为市场平台的资源有限，如果同时有太多团队参与开发，最终会互相阻碍，效率低下。因此，我们当然有专门团队专注于提升卖家体验。例如，他们如何上架库存、管理销售、完成发货等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly the same transition Airbnb went through. Initially it was focus on hosts, make sure hosts are the happiest people, and do everything we need to make them happy. And then eventually the business is the customers buying the product, and you have to make sure that they're the happy people. And sometimes you have to push hosts to do things they're not as excited to do for the good of the guest side.
turns.zh: 这与Airbnb经历的转变如出一辙。最初Airbnb专注于房东，确保房东满意，竭尽全力让他们开心。但最终业务重心转向了买家体验，必须确保买家满意。有时甚至需要督促房东做一些他们不乐意做的事，以造福客人。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: And I think it's also the fact that we as the marketplace, and I'm curious if this was true at Airbnb as well, but we have the insight into information, into data, that an individual seller won't. And so we can help them make hopefully better decisions that lead to sales, leveraging the insights that we have. (00:24:06): If you put an item on sale during this time period, chances are it's going to resonate with buyers, and you might get an incremental sale. And so trying to be really data-driven in how we help and guide sellers to take actions that we really believe will be valuable for them and their business, because simply, they're either a small business owner and so they don't have time to do that level of digging. Or it's simply not accessible to them because they have the worldview of their business, and we're looking at the entirety of the marketplace.
