(00:36:46): But the through line is, is the change that we're making adding value? And that's what we want to try to understand. A/B testing is a great way to do that. There are others, some of which we're starting to employ, others that we we'll continue to investigate and think about how we can leverage.
turns.zh: 如今，我们绝大多数的改进措施都是如此。说实话，我认为这正是我们作为产品团队乃至整个公司在增长方面的一个优势——引入多样化的验证方式。因为在某种程度上，或者说以我对实验的理解来看，这才是最高标准。它能以近乎百分之百的确定性证明，你所做的改进与你希望提升的关键绩效指标之间存在因果关系。 [新段落] 但我认为，在某些改进措施或某些领域，这或许会偏离重点。比如，当你致力于打造一个全新的东西时，或者某个特定改进措施并不能真正反映你正在构建的整体愿景。 (00:36:14): 正如我之前提到的，我们长期以来一直非常依赖A/B测试，这不仅因为Etsy的背景和历史深深植根于卓越的工程文化中，也是因为它确实行之有效。因此，绝大多数事情都是以这种方式进行测试的。 (00:36:33): 我们正在拓展对随时间变化的用户群体的思考方式。我之前提到的用户留存率，在某种程度上，它需要一种不同的测试方式。当我们审视SEO工作时，你不能用完全相同的方式去思考。 (00:36:46): 但核心问题是，我们所做的改进是否增加了价值？这才是我们想要探究的。A/B测试是实现这一目标的绝佳方式。当然，还有其他方法，我们已经开始尝试其中一些，还会继续探索并思考如何加以利用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of anything? And if there's not, that's totally cool, of something that you shipped that was maybe negative on an experiment results, or you just didn't want to write as an experiment.
turns.zh: 你能举个例子吗？如果没有，那完全没关系。比如某个实验结果可能是负面的，或者你只是不想把它写成实验。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: When we're collecting inputs from sellers, we just simply don't feel it's appropriate to not either show or honor. We talk about a tried and true practice of sales and discounting. If a seller offers something on sale, then we need to show that. We are really curious about how that actually drives buyer behavior. And there's ways that we can kind of construct pre-post analysis and things like that to try to understand the impact. But ultimately, those are the kind of areas where we err on the side looking at our data in different ways. And so we have maybe a slightly different degree of confidence in the value, but we're still confident that it does help the marketplace as a whole.
turns.zh: 在收集卖家反馈时，我们认为不展示或不重视他们的意见是不合适的。我们谈论的是销售和折扣的既定做法。如果卖家提供促销商品，那么我们就需要展示这一信息。我们真的很想了解这如何实际影响买家行为。当然，我们可以构建实验前后分析等方法来理解其影响。但归根结底，在这些领域，我们倾向于以不同的方式分析数据。因此，我们对其价值的信心程度可能稍有不同，但我们仍然确信它确实对整个市场有益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great example. Yeah, I'm not sure what I do there. That is tricky. So we've been talking about conversion. I'm curious in terms of acquisition, what you've seen work. And just generally, how do people find Etsy? How do you drive top of funnel for Etsy?
turns.zh: 这就是一个很好的例子。是的，我不确定该怎么做。这确实很棘手。所以我们一直在讨论转化率。我很好奇在获客方面，你们有什么有效的做法。总的来说，人们是如何找到Etsy的？你们如何提升Etsy的入口流量？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yes. There's two sides to Etsy, right? There's the seller and the buyer. Getting in the Wayback Machine, on the seller side, we would be at craft fairs like Renegade and other places where our sellers were selling in person and really letting them know that Etsy exists. And so that was very boots on the ground, let's get out and try to acquire sellers into the marketplace. Some of that predates me to some degree. We were probably doing it on the tail end when I joined. (00:38:37): And then we have a lot of great word of mouth through our sellers. A seller probably knows other people who are similarly inclined to be incredible craftspeople, who want to sell their items. And so we've seen some success with our... We have a Teams platform where sellers can come together, ask each other questions, and the word of mouth type of growth through that. (00:38:56): On the buyer side, we really leveraged the fact that we have a ton of inventory. And to some degree, it ends up being quite a long tail of inventory where we can meet really niche and specific needs. And so that lends itself really well to thinking about SEO, lends itself really well to thinking about Google Shopping, where someone is not on Etsy, but is often looking for something either somewhat or very specific. And we can really meet their needs in a really meaningful way by showing them not only just a single item, but maybe that and then other options that they might find that are of a similar vein, in a similar, sub categories in some cases. And so those have been long tried and true areas that we've invested in, and we've seen really great success in driving new buyers to Etsy.
turns.zh:
是的。Etsy有两个方面，对吧？一方是卖家，另一方是买家。回顾早期阶段，在卖家方面，我们会参加像Renegade这样的手工艺品展会等活动，当面向卖家推广Etsy，让他们真正了解这个平台的存在。这就是实地推广，亲自走出去，努力吸引卖家入驻。有些策略在我加入之前就已经实施了，我们加入时可能已经接近尾声了。（00:38:37）  
然后通过卖家，我们获得了大量口碑推荐。一个卖家很可能认识其他有相似兴趣、想出售自己作品的工匠。因此，我们在吸引新卖家方面取得了一定的成功。我们有一个Teams平台，卖家可以在那里交流问题，通过这种方式实现口碑传播。（00:38:56）  
在买家方面，我们充分利用了我们拥有大量库存这一优势。在某种程度上，这些库存形成了一个长尾效应，我们能够满足非常细分和特定的需求。这非常适合SEO策略，也适合Google Shopping平台，因为有些人虽然不在Etsy上，但往往在寻找某种特定的商品。我们不仅能为他们展示单个商品，还能推荐类似的商品，甚至是同一子类别中的其他选项。这些都是我们长期投入且取得显著成效的领域，我们成功地为Etsy吸引了大量新买家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've researched and written about that story of how Etsy started with sellers and craft fairs. And so that's a really classic story. And I think there's also an element of the early sellers drove the early buyers, because they're just advertising their listing page, "Here's where you could go buying," which is a really unfair rare, opportunity to grow the marketplace by just focusing on sellers.
turns.zh: 我研究并撰写过Etsy如何从卖家和手工艺品展会起步的故事。这是一个非常经典的故事。我认为早期卖家推动了早期买家的增长也存在一定的因素，因为他们只是在宣传自己的列表页面，"这里是你们可以购买的地方"，这是一个通过专注于卖家来发展市场的绝佳且不公平的机会。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I mean, yes, and a seller is a buyer. And so if they're making something that they've poured their heart into, chances are they will value that exact same behavior in someone else. And so if they're selling an item, they're looking for other things in maybe not their exact category, but in adjacent categories, and they become buyers. So it is a nice dynamic when that starts to work.
turns.zh: 是的，卖家就是买家。所以如果他们倾注心血制作某件商品，他们很可能会重视其他人同样的行为。例如，如果他们在销售一件商品，他们可能会寻找不属于自己类别但相邻类别中的其他商品，然后成为买家。当这种良性循环开始运作时，确实是一个很好的动态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So many natural advantages to getting this marketplace off the ground. How cool is that? You mentioned word of mouth as a big part of how Etsy started spreading. I imagine even today there's a lot of just, "Hey, you should check out Etsy." Is there anything you've done that accelerates word of mouth or build on word of mouth, referrals comes to mind? Is there anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 是的。让这个市场起步有很多天然优势。这多酷啊？你提到口碑是Etsy早期传播的重要部分。我想即使在今天，仍然有很多"你应该看看Etsy"的推荐。有没有你做过的加速口碑传播或基于口碑的措施，比如推荐？有没有这方面的做法？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, we dabbled with referral programs a while ago, probably eight some years ago. What we saw, it was a different time. And so I think we maybe didn't value a new buyer, for example, in the way we do today. Because to some degree, you're unlocking future value. They make a single purchase, and then the bet is over time they'll go on to make subsequent purchases. We didn't necessarily have that as deep an understanding then as we do now. So our buyer referral program ultimately wasn't a huge success. (00:41:15): But on the seller side, this was back in the days of Dropbox referral program being a huge, huge driver of their growth, and the whole get concept that was really prevalent back then. And on the seller side, one of the things that we really leaned into was, on Etsy, for those who aren't familiar, it costs 20 cents to list an item. (00:41:36): And that may seem like a very small financial outlay to get started, but it's a little bit of a barrier. And the more we can do to remove those, the higher chance that someone will either become a seller or list more items. (00:41:51): So we really leaned into that as the currency for the seller referral program. And coming back to what I said around Teams, that was a really great way to supercharge some of that activity that was either happening, but more of it could happen, or really helping a seller understand, "Oh yeah, there is a hook here. If I offer this person, I refer them, they'll get some listing credits. It'll be easier for them to open their shop. And then when I need to list more items, I also have credits that I can apply." So that was one small area. I wouldn't say it was a huge driver of growth. But in certain markets, in certain pockets, we saw it work pretty well.
turns.zh: 是的，我们曾在不久前尝试过推荐计划，大概八年前吧。但当时情况不同了。所以我觉得我们当时对新用户的重视程度可能不如现在。比如说，因为你是在挖掘他们未来的价值——他们可能只会买一次，但随着时间推移会继续购买。但当时我们对这方面的理解还不够深入。所以我们的买家推荐计划最终并不算成功。（00:41:15）但在卖家方面，当时Dropbox的推荐计划是推动其增长的巨大动力，而“裂变增长”这个概念在当时非常流行。在卖家端，我们重点关注了Etsy平台——可能有些人不熟悉，Etsy上上架一项商品需要20美分。这看似是一个很小的入门门槛，但确实存在一定障碍。只要我们能尽可能消除这些障碍，人们成为卖家或上架更多商品的可能性就会大大增加。（00:41:36）所以我们把这作为卖家推荐计划的激励机制。回到我之前提到的Teams，它是增强用户活跃度的绝佳工具。有些用户可能已经在使用，但我们可以通过它让更多人参与进来，或者帮助卖家理解：“原来还有这样的机制。如果我推荐某人，他们就能获得上架积分，这样就能更轻松地开店了。当我需要上架更多商品时，这些积分还能用于抵扣。”这只是一个小举措。虽然它并不能成为增长的核心驱动力，但在某些市场、某些细分领域，我们发现它效果不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That also helps with fraud, which is a huge problem with referral programs where the credit is just, you can list on Etsy. It's not like you can steal a lot of money away from the business. So that's clever.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这还能防止欺诈，因为推荐计划中的积分只能用于Etsy平台，用户无法从平台窃取大量资金。这设计得真巧妙。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to talk about one other part of the funnel, retention. Is there anything you've learned that has been really effective to help with the retention?
turns.zh: 好的。我想再聊聊用户留存环节。你有没有什么成功经验可以分享？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: We have long had features that are retentive in their nature. Things like, on Etsy, we call them favorites. That might be liking or a similar action on other places. But how do we think about the habit loop of if you take an action, what's the trigger and then what's the reward? [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And so using a favorite as an example, you favorite an item. That's a pretty strong ish... Of course, adding it to your cart or maybe purchasing it, that's the strongest of signals, but you've shown intent. (00:43:21): So what can we do with that information? We can then say, "The seller put it on sale. You should come back and check it out. This is selling out. There's only one of this item left. You showed some intent, you might want to come back and get it." And that's just one example of trying to close those loops. (00:43:35): And that's where we've worked on things like, we call it the updates feed, essentially a feed of activity that you've taken, that we're demonstrating how it's changed, what's new, and then pulling in the tried and true tactic of push notifications to make you aware of that, such that you're using your phone all the time. You see that show up. That's a pretty great notification to get right. "The thing that I really liked is now on sale. I want to check that out." (00:44:00): And so those are examples where really leaning into that habit loop framework has helped us understand, we've got a lot of this activity. How do we close the loop? How do we make it really valuable for our buyers?
turns.zh:
长期以来，我们一直拥有一些本质上具有留存性的功能。比如在Etsy上，我们称之为"收藏夹"。这在其他平台上可能表现为点赞或类似操作。但我们该如何理解用户行为的习惯闭环——即用户采取某个行动后，触发因素是什么，奖励又是什么？[新段落]  
以收藏夹为例，当用户收藏某件商品时，这是一个相当强烈的信号……当然，将商品加入购物车或直接购买才是最强烈的信号，但用户已经展现了意向。（00:43:21）  
那么如何利用这些信息呢？我们可以这样说：“卖家降价了，您应该回来看看。这件商品即将售罄，库存仅剩一件。您曾表现出意向，或许想回来抢购。” 这只是尝试闭合用户行为闭环的例子。（00:43:35）  
这正是我们致力于打造“动态推送流”的原因。本质上，这是一个展示用户行为动态的信息流，我们会突出变化和新内容，并借助推送通知的经典策略提醒用户，促使他们持续使用手机查看通知。例如：“我之前很喜欢的商品现在降价了，快来看看吧。” （00:44:00）  
因此，深挖用户行为闭环框架有助于我们理解现有的大量用户活动：如何闭合闭环？如何让这一切对买家真正有价值？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Zooming out a little bit, it's kind of wild that Etsy can exist in a world of eBay and Amazon. And I'm just curious what it is that you think the founders and the team did early on to carve out this space of, I know you could buy things from people, you can buy things on Amazon really quickly, to create a world where Etsy builds this massive business that continues to thrive. What do you think was done so well to carve out the space?
turns.zh: 退一步看，在eBay和亚马逊的世界里，Etsy的存在本身就令人惊叹。我很好奇创始人和团队早期是如何开拓出这一市场空间的。我知道用户可以直接从个人卖家购买商品，但在亚马逊上快速下单同样方便。那么Etsy如何在竞争中脱颖而出，打造出持续繁荣的大型平台？你们认为早期做了哪些出色的工作？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I think that to some degree, resolves down to... And maybe that's a little too extreme, but a key component is the brand. The brand stands for something in people's minds. And that helps understand you're not going to get the same inventory on Etsy. You shouldn't expect the same inventory on Etsy as you might be looking for on eBay. It doesn't make sense to our buyers. The items that our sellers sell are unique. (00:45:07): And so I think that as the core nugget, combined with how we think about policies, and our way to some degree, maintain the integrity of the marketplace, those two things combined do set us apart. And I think if you ask many people, certainly here in the US, what they think of Etsy, a very specific image will be conjured up. That may be one that we want to evolve and build on, but it feels quite distinct. (00:45:37): And it's not the same as eBay and it's not the same as Amazon. And I think there's real deep value in that. And I wasn't here at the very beginning, but it's certainly something that was there at the very beginning of Etsy, that is still a through line to where we are today.
turns.zh:
我认为这在某种程度上归结于……或许说得有些极端，但品牌是关键因素。品牌在人们心目中代表着某种价值。这有助于用户理解Etsy上的商品库存不同于eBay。买家不应期待在Etsy上找到与eBay上相同的商品库存。这对用户来说毫无意义。Etsy卖家出售的商品都是独一无二的。（00:45:07）  
所以我认为核心要素在于政策制定，以及我们在一定程度上维护市场诚信的努力。两者相结合使我们脱颖而出。我相信如果问许多人，尤其是在美国的人，他们对Etsy的印象会很具体。这或许是我们需要发展和深化的，但它确实独树一帜。（00:45:37）  
它与eBay不同，与亚马逊不同。我认为这其中蕴含着巨大价值。我虽然不在创始团队，但这正是Etsy创立之初就存在的核心要素，至今仍是我们发展的主线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes absolute sense to me. On the other hand, I also don't know how that happens. Is there anything that you think about, of how the team did that and how they built that brand? What are some of the important elements? Is that a specific aesthetic? Is it a certain type of supply that you stuck to? What do you think was so important to building that brand?
turns.zh: 这一点我完全理解。但另一方面，我也不明白这是怎么做到的。关于团队如何做到这一点，以及如何打造这个品牌，您有没有什么想法？有哪些关键要素？是特定的审美风格吗？还是坚持某种特定的供应模式？您认为打造这个品牌最重要的因素是什么？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I think it is the supply. If you think about the marketplace, the vast majority of content is maybe what we might consider UGC. It's either the item is from the seller. Or as was mentioning before, the buyer review is from the buyer. And so just being really clear about what's okay to sell and what's not okay, I think does really differentiate us. (00:46:38): I also think over the years, our brand, and our aesthetic, and how we position ourselves has evolved, will continue to evolve as it should. But to the point where we are now, the statement we have is keep commerce human. And that feels really simple, super pithy, easy to remember, but has lineage when you go all the way back to where we started in terms of really valuing the unique, valuing the handmade. And so that does permeate decision making, how we show up, the type of features we work on, the things we would prioritize. Maybe never say never, but an item getting dropped off by a drone and a person never touches it, that doesn't feel very Etsy. That's not something that we might lean into.
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于供应。如果你看看整个市场，大多数内容可能都属于用户生成内容（UGC）。商品要么来自卖家，要么像之前提到的，买家评价来自买家。因此，明确哪些商品可以销售，哪些不可以，确实能让我们脱颖而出。（00:46:38）：我还认为，多年来，我们的品牌、审美以及定位方式一直在发展，并且还会继续发展。但就目前而言，我们的理念是“让电商回归人性化”。这听起来很简单、很简洁，也容易让人记住，但它源于我们最初的价值观——重视独特性、手工制作。这种理念贯穿于我们的决策、品牌形象、开发的功能以及优先事项中。或许永远不排除可能性，但无人机送货、商品从未经过人工检查，这感觉不像Etsy的风格。我们不会大力推广这种模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how many parallels Etsy has to Airbnb, because Airbnb is the same general idea. People's homes, people making things. And then also, I think the tagline for Airbnb early on was travel like a human. So it was actually a really similar concept.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，Etsy和Airbnb有很多相似之处，因为Airbnb的核心理念也差不多——人们的家、手工制作。另外，Airbnb早期的标语是“像人类一样旅行”，这两个理念其实很相似。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which touches on a question I wanted to talk about, which is many marketplaces as they grow, become supply constrained. And then there's this pressure to add different types of supply. In Airbnb's case, it was, "We should add hotels, we should add property management, vacation rental companies on here. We should have everything people want to book, because we're losing business. They could book anything here, they should be able to." But the tension is, then we become like everyone else. And then what is Airbnb in that case? (00:48:04): And I think you went through that experience where there was a lot of cheap products from overseas, and it was kind of being flooded. Is that true, I guess? And then just how do you think about that limit, and where you draw that line?
turns.zh: 这让我想到了一个我想探讨的问题，许多市场平台在发展过程中会面临供应受限的问题。然后就面临着增加不同类型供应的压力。在Airbnb的案例中，他们曾想：“我们应该增加酒店、物业管理、度假租赁公司。用户需要预订各种东西，因为我们正在失去市场份额。他们应该能在这里预订任何想预订的服务。”但问题是，这样一来我们就和其他平台没什么区别了。那样的Airbnb还算Airbnb吗？（00:48:04）：我记得你们也经历过海外廉价商品大量涌入的阶段。这是真的吗？那你们是如何划定界限，设定底线的？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, I think it does come back to some degree to the brand and the policy point from just before. And we take enforcing our policies really seriously. It's not an easy job at our scale, and that means we need to continue to invest and continue to make sure that only the best items, the most relevant items are on Etsy. That job is never done. The team that that works super, super hard, and is always looking for new signals to understand what maybe doesn't meet our criteria. (00:48:49): Generally speaking, supply is something that we have in spades for the most part. Back to the point we talked about earlier, one of the things that we grappled with was around, how can we help sellers scale? They sell great inventory, but maybe they just don't have enough of it, or they can't meet the demand, because they're making everything by hand. (00:49:10): So one of the things that there was an evolution, was leaning into what today we call production assistance. And the way I think about that is you still need to understand the provenance of your item. If you are saying, "I have this design, I'm just going to throw it over the fence to a manufacturer that I've never met, that I don't know. I don't understand their processes, I may not agree with them," that doesn't meet our criteria. You need to understand how it's being made, who is making it, have a relationship with the person who's helping you scale your business. But that's something that we saw from people who maybe gravitate more towards being designers than being able to actually make the thing. They have this excellent idea, they just can't see it come to life. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And so they need some help. And that was something we leaned into to be able to, like I said, help sellers that maybe weren't able to make a thing and sell it on Etsy. Or for sellers who were reaching the limits of what they could supply, really take it to the next level, and make more items such that they could make more sales.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这在一定程度上确实回归到品牌和之前提到的政策层面。我们非常认真地执行我们的政策。以我们的规模来说，这绝非易事，这意味着我们需要持续投入，确保只有最优质、最相关的商品能在Etsy上售卖。这项工作永无止境。我们的团队非常努力，总是在寻找新的信号，以判断哪些商品可能不符合我们的标准。（00:48:49）：一般来说，供应方面我们基本上不存在问题。回到我们之前讨论的要点，我们曾面临的一个难题是，如何帮助卖家实现规模化发展？他们可能有很棒的库存，但可能因为是手工制作而无法满足需求。（00:49:10）：所以我们做出了调整，推出了如今所谓的生产协助服务。我对此的理解是，你仍然需要了解商品的来源。如果你说：“我有这个设计，就把它扔给一个从未见过、互不了解的制造商，他们的工艺我不了解，可能也不认同”，这就不符合我们的标准。你需要了解商品的制作过程，了解制作者，并与帮助你扩大业务规模的人建立关系。但我们发现，有些人更倾向于做设计师，而非实际制作产品。他们有绝佳的创意，却无法将其变为现实。[新段落]因此他们需要帮助。这正是我们致力于帮助那些可能无法在Etsy上销售商品的卖家，或是那些已达到供应极限、急需提升产能的卖家所需的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like essentially, this is just evolving definition of what a supplies allowed on Etsy, a team that stays on top of that. Imagine there was just a hard decision at one point of just, "We will limit supply, and here's the supply that we want on the platform. Everything else we're going to take off."
turns.zh: 所以听起来基本上，这就是对Etsy上允许供应的商品定义的不断演变，而团队始终紧跟其后。想象一下，如果曾经有一个硬性决定：“我们将限制供应，以下是我们希望在平台上出现的供应商品。其他所有商品都将下架。”

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: We would limit the type of items, the number of those items, that as we talked about, there's a lot of them. But really having that clear definition. In some cases, it's easy. Some things, they violate legal definitions. And those things, that's the easy stuff to think about. It's where it's a little more gray, that it gets a little trickier.
turns.zh: 我们会限制商品类型和数量，正如我们之前讨论的，这类商品数量众多。但真正需要明确定义。在某些情况下，这很简单。有些商品违反了法律定义。这些问题相对容易处理。但有些情况则比较模糊，处理起来更棘手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me, so my wife is actually a designer, and she produces these hilarious charts about life stuff. And people take her designs and just sell them on every platform on Zazzle, and probably Etsy, but everywhere. And she's always trying to hunt them down and get them to take them off. But it's such a pain for a small designer. It's not an Etsy problem, it's just a general internet problem.
turns.zh: 这让我想起，我妻子实际上是一名设计师，她制作了许多关于生活琐事的搞笑图表。人们拿走她的设计，在Zazzle、Etsy等各个平台上销售。但她总是在追查并要求下架。但对于小设计师来说，这实在太麻烦了。这不是Etsy的问题，而是整个互联网普遍存在的问题。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah. And back to the, we have teams hard at work thinking about IP, and how to police it, how to enforce it.
turns.zh: 是的。回到我们所说的，我们有团队正在努力思考知识产权问题，以及如何监管和执行相关规定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's tough.
turns.zh: 这很困难。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Not a domain I will suggest I'm an expert in, really, really tricky stuff, but we've got to be beyond that.
turns.zh: 这不是我会自诩擅长的领域，确实是件棘手的事，但我们必须超越这些难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Another I think problem that's sort of unique to Etsy, something that I think people call the graduation problem. Which is where you join Etsy, things start to grow, you become really successful. And then you're like, "Why am I paying Etsy all these fees? Why don't I just make my own website and just sell it directly, and not pay any fees?" And I think you guys went through that. And so if that's true, is there anything you've learned about just how to avoid getting people to want to leave?
turns.zh: 是的。我认为Etsy独有的一个问题，就是所谓的“毕业问题”。当你加入Etsy后，业务开始发展壮大，变得非常成功。但随后你就会想：“为什么要给Etsy交那么多费用呢？为什么不自己建个网站，直接销售，省去这些费用呢？”我觉得你们也经历过这个阶段。那么，如果这种情况确实存在，你们有没有总结出如何避免用户想离开的经验？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I think the core thought there is, our fees are generally low and highly competitive. So from that perspective, there's a reason to stay on Etsy. What we've seen and what we know, our sellers are really smart business people. And so if they can distribute their products through another channel, that might be their own website, another marketplace in person. Probably going to try to do that. They want to make more sales. Not all, but many of them are wired to want to grow their business. (00:52:21): And so really understanding the role that we play in that construct of distribution channels to make it a little reductive is really helpful to understand. And to some degree, we want to be the place that not only they make sales on, but they love to sell on, because our tools are really catered to the needs that they have. (00:52:42): So there is some degree of stickiness. I mentioned Teams earlier. There are places where sellers go to congregate, share ideas, share grievances in some cases, but ultimately support each other. And so there are reasons to stick around. I'm sure there certainly sellers who scale out of Etsy who realize, "I want to build my own website," to the example you cited. The reality is that's neither cheap nor fast. It's hard work. It's hard work to build, hard work to maintain, expensive to drive traffic to. And so that may be a part of the way they want to take their business, but oftentimes, Etsy still does play a role in how they're thinking, about where they make sales, and ultimately where they're going to see growth from.
turns.zh: 我认为核心观点是，我们的费用总体上很低，极具竞争力。从这个角度来看，在Etsy上继续发展是合理的。根据我们的观察和了解，卖家们都是非常精明的商人。如果他们能通过其他渠道分销产品，比如自己的网站、其他市场、线下销售，很多人都会尝试这么做。他们希望获得更多销售量。虽然不是所有人，但很多卖家都渴望拓展业务。（00:52:21）因此，真正理解我们在分销渠道体系中所扮演的角色——简而言之，理解我们如何为他们提供支持——对理解他们的需求非常有帮助。在某种程度上，我们希望成为他们不仅能销售产品，还乐于销售产品的平台，因为我们的工具真正满足了他们的需求。（00:52:42）所以确实存在一定的粘性。前面我提到了Teams。有些地方是卖家聚集、分享想法、倾诉困扰的地方，但最终大家还是会互相支持。所以他们有理由留下来。我相信确实有卖家从Etsy扩展出去后，意识到“我想建自己的网站”，比如你提到的例子。但现实是，这既不便宜也不容易。建设和维护网站需要大量工作，引流成本也很高。所以虽然这可能是他们拓展业务的方向，但Etsy在他们的销售渠道和增长策略中仍然发挥着重要作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The cool thing that I saw online about you, is that you built a marketplace essentially within Etsy called Etsy Studio. And I'm not sure if that's around anymore, but I'm curious what the story there was, and what you learned from that experience, and current status.
turns.zh: 我在网上看到关于你们的有趣之处，是在Etsy内部建立了一个名为Etsy Studio的市场。我不确定它现在是否还在运营，但我很好奇背后的故事、从中吸取的经验以及它目前的状况。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, well researched. Because no, it is no longer around. The white space we saw with studio was essentially saying, on the one hand you've got Pinterest fails, right? You've got all these great inspiring items or projects on Pinterest, and then you have people who've no idea how to make them, and they get so frustrated. (00:54:01): And then on the other hand, you've got a marketplace like Michael's, or these other places where you might go for craft supplies. They have stuff, but they don't necessarily have inspiration. And how can we play in that intersection of the idea and the items and the tutorials to see that idea come to life? (00:54:21): So the genesis of the idea, felt from a brand perspective, super aligned. We stand for creativity, we stand for makers. And so we saw it as a big opportunity. The launch happened to coincide with the pivot in 2017, to really focusing on the core marketplace or refocusing on the core marketplace, maybe I should say. (00:54:41): And so it became clear that when we laid out what we're optimizing for, which is driving sales in the short term, marketing dollars being as ROI positive as possible, having teams focused on the core marketplace, it didn't check any of those boxes. And so really, really tough decision and hard to manage through, but that was ultimately the right call for the business to say, "This no longer makes sense given the new constraints that we're operating in, given the new goals that we have."
turns.zh: 是的，研究得很透彻。但不幸的是，这个项目现在已经停掉了。我们之前看到的Studio平台存在的空白，本质上是这样的：一方面，你在Pinterest上看到各种很棒的灵感项目或创意，但很多人不知道怎么实现这些创意，最后只能灰心丧气。（00:54:01）另一方面，你去Michael's这类手工艺品市场，虽然有材料可选，但往往缺乏灵感启发。那么如何在创意、材料和教程之间找到交集，让这些创意真正落地呢？（00:54:21）从品牌角度来看，这个创意的诞生非常契合我们的定位。我们倡导创造力，支持手工艺者。因此我们认为这是一个绝佳的机遇。2017年业务转型时，我们决定重新聚焦核心市场平台，这个决定再合适不过了。（00:54:41）但当我们审视优化目标时，比如短期销售增长、营销ROI最大化，以及团队专注核心业务时，发现这个项目与这些目标完全不符。最终，我们不得不艰难地做出决定，承认在新环境、新目标下，这个项目已然不合时宜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. Also something that happened to Airbnb a lot, trying new things that they didn't work out, had to move on.
turns.zh: 有道理。Airbnb也经常遇到这种情况，尝试新项目失败后不得不转向其他方向。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's how it goes.
turns.zh: 这就是现实。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shifting a little bit to just product leadership and writing the product team, and just a few more questions, what's something that you've found to be really important to having a productive, well run, well executing product team?
turns.zh: 稍微转向产品领导和产品团队管理，再问几个问题。你认为对于一个高效、运作良好的产品团队来说，哪些因素最为重要？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah. One of the things that's certainly not completely novel but I think we have a pretty unique interpretation of is how we collaborate between functions. You'll often hear the three legs of the stool where you've got product and engine design,, and we've evolved that to five legs of the stool. And I fully recognize that a five legged stool probably is not a very stable thing, but go with the analogy for a second-
turns.zh: 是的。其中一个不算新颖的观点，但我们有独特的理解，就是跨职能协作。我们常听到“三条腿的凳子”理论，即产品、工程和设计，但我们把它扩展到了“五条腿的凳子”。我承认五条腿的凳子可能不稳，但先顺着这个比喻说吧——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's even more stable. Is that the most stable stool or is it less stable with five legs?
turns.zh: 我觉得它更稳。五条腿的凳子更稳还是更不稳？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: You probably need a really flat surface.
turns.zh: 可能需要一个非常平整的表面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense.
turns.zh: 有道理。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Regardless, of course we've got product eng design and we've got our insights partners. So research and analytics, and we've got our marketing partners really working in a tight team to build the best products possible. And so I think that we can continue to get better absolutely, at how we make decisions and how we bring the various viewpoints together. So to some degree it's not the easiest path, but it's the best path I think, where you're really incorporating different viewpoints, different constraints, different considerations into the features and the products that we're building. And treating that as the core leadership team I think is really valuable. (00:56:45): And maybe that's partly because generally, we don't subscribe to this idea of PM as the mini CEO. You're up there directing from on high that we're going to build that feature and we're going to do that. And that's just not the type of culture that we have, and generally speaking from what I've seen, doesn't lead to good decisions or the best features or product being built. And so collaboration is something we really value and that we try to live through how we structure our teams, how we make our decisions. Is it perfect? Like I said, absolutely not. I think it's the way that we've found being really successful building product.
turns.zh:
无论如何，我们当然有产品工程设计团队，也有洞察力合作伙伴。因此，研究和分析部门，以及我们的营销合作伙伴确实在紧密合作，共同打造尽可能出色的产品。我认为我们肯定能在决策制定和整合不同观点方面不断提升。就某种程度而言，这条路并不容易，但我认为这是最佳之路——你要真正将不同的观点、不同的制约因素和不同考量因素融入到我们正在开发的功能和产品中。在我看来，将这视为核心领导团队的做法非常有价值。  
（00:56:45）：或许部分原因在于，我们通常不认同产品经理是"迷你CEO"的观点——你站在高处发号施令，要求开发某个功能或执行某项任务。但这不是我们所秉持的文化类型。就我观察所得，这种文化通常无法催生出优质的决策或出色的产品。因此，合作是我们极为重视的，并通过团队架构和决策流程来践行这一理念。它是否完美？如我所言，绝对不完美。但我认为这是我们成功打造产品的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you give the PM just a little more say in decision making and ask? Because with five people in the leadership team, you talked about how back in the day, it was like too consensus driven maybe, and I wonder how you navigate that with five decision makers.
turns.zh: 您是否会让产品经理在决策中拥有更大的话语权？因为领导团队有五人，您曾提到过去可能过于追求共识，我想知道在五位决策者中如何协调。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, we're always looking to clarify, or re-clarify, or restate who ultimately is accountable. And in many cases it is the PM, right? You are the one who Nick, our CPO like to say you don't have to have the best ideas, but you have to choose the best ideas. And so really figuring out how you're selecting what you're going to build and then living with the consequences. (00:58:00): Of course ideally, successful. In many cases, back to your 80% stat that 80% of experiments don't work, owning what's next, right? Okay, did we learn from that? If we did, what are we going to do about it? That definitely does fall to the PM. It doesn't give you the permission to ignore other viewpoints or make decisions in a vacuum. It's certainly not that. But ultimately, when we need to move forward, it is the PM that is on the hook for those things.
turns.zh: 是的，我们一直在努力明确或重新明确职责归属。在许多情况下，责任最终由产品经理承担。对吧？正如我们的首席产品官尼克所说，产品经理不必拥有最佳创意，但必须选择最佳方案。因此，真正要考虑的是如何筛选出要开发的功能，并承担后果。（00:58:00）：理想情况下，成功是目标。但正如您提到的80%实验失败的数据，接下来的方向由谁来把握？好的，我们从中吸取了教训吗？如果有，我们该如何改进？这无疑是产品经理的职责。这并不意味着可以忽视其他观点或在真空中做决策。绝非如此。但最终，当我们需要推进时，产品经理必须为此负责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So essentially, the PM can make the call if there's an unclear consensus?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以基本上，如果存在不明确的共识，产品经理可以做出决定？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: And given so many places are, but we're so heavily led by the insights either qual or quant. The decision in many instances is clear. When it's not, that's when we need the product person to step forward and say, "We're going in this direction." Don't know if it's going to work out, but we'll certainly learn and we'll move forward.
turns.zh: 鉴于许多公司都严重依赖定性或定量洞察，但我们在很大程度上受洞察团队主导。多数情况下决策是明确的。当不明确时，产品经理就需要站出来，说：“我们将朝这个方向前进。”不确定是否会成功，但我们肯定会从中学习并继续前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And then just to go on this topic a little bit more, your teams are cross-functional dedicated teams. I imagine it sounds like there's these five leads for each team. Is that roughly how you organize?
turns.zh: 太棒了。再多谈谈这个话题。您的团队是跨职能的专职团队。我想听起来每个团队都有五位负责人。大致是这样组织的吗？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah. And the fifth leg, if you will, of marketing, that might be product marketing in some cases, that might be brand marketing in others. And so there's kind of different flavors of marketing that we pull in, based on the specific needs of the project. But that's generally speaking how we try to structure our teams from kind of the group level all the way down to the individual squad. We can't always have a dedicated research, and a dedicated analyst, and a dedicated product marketer to every single team. So it's certainly not perfect, but that's where we aspire to having at least coverage on those roles.
turns.zh: 是的。如果要说第五个营销环节，在某些情况下可能是产品营销，在其他情况下可能是品牌营销。因此，根据项目的具体需求，我们会引入不同类型的营销策略。但总的来说，我们会从团队层面到个人小组，努力构建合理的团队架构。我们无法为每个团队都配备专门的研究人员、分析师和产品营销人员，所以这肯定不是完美的，但我们至少会确保这些职位在团队中有所覆盖。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So most teams have dedicated marketing person or a product marketing person. That's crazy. That's really rare, but interesting.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以大多数团队都有专门的营销人员或产品营销人员。这太不可思议了。这真的很罕见，但很有趣。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Some teams-
turns.zh: 有些团队——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some teams that I imagine are most in need of marketing support. Got it. Are you able to just paint a rough picture of the way the teams are laid out at Etsy? I imagine there's a buyer side and a seller side. How does that look for people to make sense-
turns.zh: 有些团队，我想他们最需要营销支持。明白了。你能否大致描述一下Etsy团队的架构？我猜应该有买家端和卖家端。能否简单说明一下——

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah. The way that we think about the structure right now, and the org design should ideally follow strategy. And if your strategy is always evolving, then your org design is always evolving. We call it the product stack. And so we've got our core customer teams, who are unsurprisingly thinking about buyers and sellers. And so they're the ones on the front lines with the customers. (01:00:26): Then we have, we call them our partner teams, and so they are working directly with the end customer. So think an organization like payments where they have clearly a way to capture payment from a buyer to remit funds to a seller, so they're really on the front lines with the customer. They also have other constraints working with the payment networks, and card providers, and things like that, so they just have a slightly different model. So core customer, partner teams, enablement teams that are really in service of helping deliver the best possible experience. That might be through our recommender systems or through our design system, in order to make developing that little bit easier, a little bit faster, a little bit more standardized in some cases. And then the foundation of it all sits with infrastructure, and the teams that you might expect that are much more technical in nature, that really, without that, we wouldn't have a website.
turns.zh: 是的。我们目前对架构的思考方式是，组织设计最好能与战略紧密结合。如果你的战略在不断发展，那么组织架构也应该随之调整。我们称之为产品栈。核心客户团队无需多言，他们主要关注买家和卖家，是直接与客户打交道的第一线团队。（01:00:26）然后我们有所谓的合作伙伴团队，他们直接与终端客户合作。比如支付团队，他们需要处理买家支付和向卖家转账的流程，所以他们也是直接与客户打交道的第一线团队。不过他们在与支付网络、卡片提供商等合作时也面临诸多限制，因此他们的运作模式略有不同。核心客户团队、合作伙伴团队，以及支持团队，主要致力于提供最佳用户体验。这可能通过我们的推荐系统或设计系统来实现，目的是让开发更高效、更标准化。基础设施团队则奠定了所有工作的根基，他们负责的技术性工作若没有这些团队支持，我们的网站根本无法运行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you're hiring a product manager, is there anything that you found to be really important or interesting, or maybe a unique insight into hiring teams?
turns.zh: 在招聘产品经理时，有没有什么特别重要或有趣的点？或者在团队招聘方面有没有独特的见解？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: The three things that I come back to time and again, is one, the collaboration piece that we talked about earlier. Not only a willingness, but a real excitement to do that. It's not everyone's bag. I get that. Some people just want to be in a make fast decisions and move forward place. We aim to make fast decisions, but you need to consult. That's one. (01:01:49): Two is being decisive. We have tons of data, but it's not always clear exactly what to do with that, or we're using a new input. Maybe back to the point mentioned earlier of looking at competitive insights, let's make a decision, let's move forward. Let's ideally learn. Even if we're not making progress against our goals, we're at a minimum learning. (01:02:10): And then the third point is just curiosity. Because we're a relatively small organization with... Everyone says, "If only we had more people," but we are quite small. (01:02:20): So there is a lot of change. There's a lot of new priorities that crop up, and that means there's a lot of opportunity for the right folks, right? If I want to be in this space, and only this space, and this is my specific domain, and I just want to be in it forever more, that might be a little more challenging, because you might be asked to work on something net new. And so just having that curiosity mindset of saying, or maybe said differently growth mindset of, "Okay, there's something to learn from the thing I'm being asked to do, let me really lean into that." (01:02:47): And to some degree, I'm not describing anything that's atypical of great product people overall. But I think we have either a slightly different flavor or we need it in a slightly different way here at Etsy.
turns.zh:
以下是用户提供的英文文本的中文翻译：

 以下是我反复提及的三件事：第一件事是我们之前讨论过的合作项目。不仅要有合作意愿，还要有真正的热情去做这件事。这并非每个人都能做到的，我理解这一点。有些人只想快速做决定、推进项目。我们也追求快速决策，但这需要充分协商。这是第一点。

（01:01:49）第二点是果断决策。我们有大量数据，但并不总是清楚该如何利用这些数据，或者我们会遇到新的输入。比如，回到之前提到的竞争洞察，迅速做出决策，推进项目，最好还能从中学习。即使我们未能朝着目标取得进展，至少也能积累经验。

（01:02:10）第三点就是保持好奇心。因为我们是一个相对较小的组织，每个人都会说：“要是我们能多些人就好了。” 但我们确实规模不大。这意味着有很多变化，新的优先事项不断涌现，这对合适的人才来说就是机会所在。假如我想专注于某个领域，只专注于这个领域，永远深耕下去，那可能更具挑战性，因为你可能会被要求参与全新的项目。因此，保持好奇心，或者用成长型思维方式看待问题——“好吧，从我被要求做的事中能学到什么，让我全身心投入其中。”——这很重要。

（01:02:47）在某种程度上，我所描述的这些并非产品经理的特质。但我认为在 Etsy 这里，我们要么有稍微不同的侧重点，要么需要以不同的方式应用这些理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Last question, before we get to our very exciting lightning round. Is there a framework or a process that you find really useful, that you find yourself coming back to, that you think listeners would potentially find really valuable?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在我们即将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题：是否有某个框架或流程对您非常有用，您经常回顾，并且认为听众可能会觉得很有价值？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I won't pretend to know whether listeners find it valuable. But the thing that I do a lot, that we do as my team, that others do to some degree is a simple exercise of weekly focus. What are you focused on this week? And then reflecting on, did you get done the things you were focused on last week? Seems super simple, but just the exercise of thinking about what matters, writing it down, and having a little bit of social proof or articulating it out to others creates some degree of accountability, is something that is very, very easy and simple to do. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]And if you do it consistently, you start to see some really great patterns of, "Those types of focus areas take me longer than I think. I should budget more time." Or, "These are the type of things that crop up. At this time of year, I might need to start thinking about making some space for them." So I've just found that to be really, really, really helpful in the day-to-day.
turns.zh: 我不敢说听众是否会觉得它有价值。但我和我的团队经常做的一件事，其他人也在一定程度上会做的，就是每周专注点设定这个简单的练习。您本周的专注点是什么？然后反思上周的专注点是否完成了？看似非常简单，但思考什么才是重要的，把它写下来，或者向他人分享以获得社会认同，形成某种程度的责任感，这确实非常简单易行。[新段落]如果持续这样做，您会开始发现一些非常好的规律，比如“某些类型的专注点比我想象的花费更长时间。我应该预留更多时间。”或者“这些类型的任务总会出现。在一年中的这个时候，我可能需要开始为它们腾出空间了。” 所以我发现这在日常工作中非常、非常、非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. How do you operationalize that? Is it like a Slack channel people post these in, is it a Docs?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个做法。您是如何将其付诸实践的？是通过 Slack 频道让大家发布这些内容，还是用文档？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah. In our buyer experience product channel, on Mondays, everyone's kind of sharing what they're focused on. How last week panned out, was it done? Is it still in progress? Things like that. It's very, very lo-fi, but it worked pretty well.
turns.zh: 是的。在我们的买家体验产品频道上，每周一，每个人都会分享他们的专注点、上周的完成情况、是否仍在进行中等等。虽然方式非常简陋，但效果不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's kind of like a standup that happens once a week, and it's higher level essentially is what it sounds like?
turns.zh: 这么说，这就像每周一次的脱口秀，而其更深层的意义基本上就是字面意思？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Exactly, exactly. Trying to think about the priorities and not tasks. And that is a blurry line. I fully recognize that. But anchoring in those I think is certainly for me, personally more helpful.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。试着去关注优先事项而非具体任务。这条界限确实模糊，我完全承认这一点。但对我个人而言，专注于优先事项确实更有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is the comedian person in these and sharing funny things in the standup-
turns.zh: 那么，在这些脱口秀中，喜剧演员会分享有趣的故事——

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: No, unfortunately, or fortunately, he's now actually a comedian.
turns.zh: 不，遗憾的是，或者说幸运的是，他现在实际上成了一名喜剧演员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you serious he became a full time comedian? That’s amazing. And with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 你说他成了全职喜剧演员？太棒了。说到这，我们迎来了激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Hit me.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Couple that come to mind Team of Teams by Stanley McChrystal has been, I think is just A, really fascinating read, and B, helped me think a lot about how you trust teams and how you think about disseminating decision-making to the right folks, tech language, push decisions to the edges. But thinking about it in the context that he describes there is really fascinating, and it just shows that it can work even in the most egregious world of military, which you think is top-down command and control, shows that there's a different way to approach problems.
turns.zh: 首先想到的是斯坦利·麦克里斯特尔的《团队的力量》。这本书读起来非常引人入胜，B部分让我深受启发，特别是他如何信任团队，如何将决策权下放给合适的人——用技术术语来说就是“将决策推向边缘”。但结合他书中描述的案例来看，这一理念令人惊叹。它甚至在军事这样等级森严的领域也能奏效，证明了用不同的方式解决问题是可行的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was actually a fan favorite at Airbnb also.
turns.zh: 我在Airbnb时也是深受大家喜爱的人物。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Oh, cool. Other is back all the way to the top to what I love to do. Surfing and being outdoors. Let My People Go Surfing by Yvon Chouinard, the Patagonia founder. Incredibly fascinating read of someone who just had a deep, deep passion, turned it into a business, struggled, iterated, came out the other side really successful. So the business side, but also just how they think about treating their employees and the culture that they've built I think is to me personally, really inspiring. There's a theme here around trust and how you engage with people to make their day-to-day work lives, is really fulfilling. So that's another favorite. And then in a super different direction, Power Broker by Robert Caro. That is an absolute tone. It is huge. It took me probably an entire year to read because I'm an extremely slow reader and/or I fell asleep a lot. But it is so fascinating, especially living in New York, of how one human had such an incredibly outsized and probably terrible impact on the city. Access to waterfronts, really thinking about communities and tearing them apart. Just such a fascinating read.
turns.zh: 哦，真酷。现在回到我最热爱的事情——冲浪和户外活动。帕塔哥尼亚创始人伊冯·乔伊纳德的《让我的员工去冲浪》。这本书读起来极其引人入胜，讲述了一个怀揣深切热情、将其转化为事业、历经挫折、不断迭代，最终成功的人物。书中关于如何对待员工以及构建企业文化的理念，对我个人而言极具启发。这里始终围绕信任展开，以及如何通过与人互动，让他们的日常工作生活充满成就感。这也是我最喜欢的书。再说一个截然不同的方向，罗伯特·卡罗的《权力掮客》。这本书绝对震撼人心。它篇幅巨大，读起来花了整整一年时间，因为我阅读速度极慢，还老是打瞌睡。但书中内容极其引人入胜，尤其是身处纽约的我们，了解一个人如何对这座城市产生如此巨大且可能有害的影响——从水fronts的开发，到社区的分裂，读来令人震撼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have that book, and I've never read it. It's very long and intimidating. I think it might be back there, maybe in a different-
turns.zh: 我有这本书，但从没读过。它太长了，让人望而生畏。我想可能把它分成几章一次性读完，否则实在难以应付。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I would chunk it out. Do a couple of chapters at a time, otherwise it feels insurmountable.
turns.zh: 我会分段处理。每次读几章，否则会觉得无从下手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like infinite Infinite Jest where you're intimidated. Amazing. Okay, next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show? Tim Holley (01:07:15) So my wife and I talk about this a lot. I think we're Western Files, if that's a thing. I'm from Europe and so it's a whole new world, different world for me. We've loved Yellowstone and all of the, I guess they're prequels. They've been just really, really fun to watch for people who are curious about that culture and that world.
turns.zh:
这就像无穷无尽的《无尽的玩笑》，让人倍感压力。太棒了。好的，下一个问题：你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？
蒂姆·霍利（01:07:15）我和妻子经常讨论这个问题。我觉得我们属于“西方档案派”，毕竟我来自欧洲，对我来说那完全是个全新的世界。《黄石》系列剧集太棒了，虽然都是前传，但对于好奇那片文化和世界的人来说，看这些剧集真的超有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. It's also been hard to find where to even watch it. It's on the weirdest channels.
turns.zh: 太棒了。但找个能看的地方真是难上加难。它在最奇怪的频道上播放。

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: It is one of those where the old world of, we cut all our cords and we only needed Netflix. Suddenly you need all these really random providers of content that you're like, "I have to subscribe to that now to watch this show?"
turns.zh: 这类内容的转变真是令人惊叹。我们以前剪断了所有线缆，只需订阅Netflix就能看剧。现在突然又需要订阅各种各样的流媒体服务，心里还想：“我现在必须为看这部剧付费？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Don't understand where this even is. Just take my money. Favorite interview question you like to ask candidates? Tim Holley (01:07:58) I'm a big fan of case studies, live case studies. I think you learn a whole boatload about how someone thinks on the fly, how they react to constraints. So we use those. I've used those a ton. We use them pretty heavily in product interviews. So I love those modulated for the type of business you're in, what you're actually trying to understand. [NEW_PARAGRAPH]The other one I like to ask is around something that people have taught themselves, tried to get at a growth mindset. I think Julia, who was on the podcast a while ago, said something similar. But you get a ton of insight into someone. Ideally, you get a bit of passion and you often get something to go research. She's like, "I don't know anything about that topic. I want to learn a little more." Lenny (01:08:40) What is a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh:
完全不知道去哪儿找。直接扣钱吧。你最喜欢问候选人的面试问题是什么？
蒂姆·霍利（01:07:58）我特别喜欢案例研究，特别是实时案例研究。通过这种方式，你能深入了解对方的即时思维方式和应对挑战的能力。我们在产品面试中大量使用这类案例。（新段落）另一个我常问的问题是关于人们自学提升的心态。前不久嘉宾朱莉娅也提到过类似观点。但通过提问，你能深入了解对方的内在动力，往往还能激发他们的热情，甚至让他们去深入探索。比如他们会说：“我对这个主题一无所知，但我想多了解一些。”
伦尼（01:08:40）你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: You as a new parent maybe resonates when... So it's not new, because our kids too. But when I was looking, being in product, of course you want to track data. And so I was looking for apps that would be good at doing that, and they nearly all look like hideous medical charts where I just don't want to engage with that. I found this one app, I think it's called Nara Baby or Nara something. Super simple, allows both parents to enter information. Probably grandparents too. We only tested it with two people. Seamlessly syncs. Really easy to use. So at 4:00 AM when you can't see and you just want to say, "I fed the baby," you can do that really easily. Just really, really simple, fit for purpose product. So that resonated with me.
turns.zh: 作为新手父母，可能感同身受吧……虽然这不算新鲜事，因为我们家孩子也是这样。但我找产品时当然想追踪数据，发现大多数应用都像难看的医疗图表，让人毫无兴趣。最后我发现Nara Baby这款应用，简单易用，父母甚至祖父母都能记录信息。我们只测试了两个人，数据无缝同步，操作极其便捷。凌晨四点你累得睁不开眼，只想记录“喂了宝宝”这样的信息，都能轻松完成。真是简洁实用的好产品。这让我深有共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to be downloading that right now. I've been using Huckleberry, which is both awesome and not awesome, and so awesome tip. Great. What is a favorite life motto that you like to repeat often or share with other people, either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我现在就去下载试试。我一直在用Huckleberry，既好用又不尽如人意，不过这确实是个很棒的建议。太棒了。你最喜欢的座右铭是什么？无论工作还是生活中，经常挂在嘴边或与人分享的？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: One of the things I talk about maybe internally more than anything else, but all or nothing. Go all in. Go do the thing. In German [German 01:10:08]. I grew up in Germany, so that's something I say to myself a lot is if you're going to do it, do it properly. I think those are often helpful words to live by.
turns.zh: 我最常谈论的，可能更多是在公司内部，但这句话适用于所有人：要么全力以赴，要么一事无成。用德语来说就是[德语 01:10:08]。我在德国长大，所以常对自己说——如果你要做，就要做得完美。这句话确实是行事的良方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Final question, what's a favorite item you recently discovered on Etsy?
turns.zh: 太喜欢了。最后一个问题，你最近在Etsy上发现的最喜欢的商品是什么？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: I recently bought an engraved whiskey decanter for my wife and myself, or for the home. Super beautiful, so cool. Got it personalized with our names. Just such a cool, cool item, that I wasn't expecting to find that kind of thing. I'm not even sure exactly how you engrave a whiskey decanter, but it was really cool. And the other thing, I'm always on the lookout for greeting cards. If anyone has great greeting card seller recommendations, I'm all ears. I love giving out physical greetings cards to folks, so that's another always on Etsy favorite of mine.
turns.zh: 我最近给妻子和我自己买了一个刻字威士忌醒酒器，或者说给家里买的。超级漂亮，太酷了。还刻上了我们的名字。这东西太酷了，完全出乎我的意料。我甚至不确定威士忌醒酒器怎么刻字的，但真的很棒。另外，我一直在寻找贺卡。如果有人有好的贺卡卖家推荐，我洗耳恭听。我喜欢给人们送实体贺卡，所以这也是我在Etsy上最喜欢的部分之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tim, we've talked about growth, culture, surfing, cabins, leadership. Thank you so much for being here. I'm downloading the Nara app right now as we speak. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 蒂姆，我们聊了成长、文化、冲浪、木屋、领导力。非常感谢你能来。我现在正在下载奈良应用。最后两个问题。粉丝们如果想联系你、了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到你？听众又如何能为你提供帮助呢？

turns.speaker: Tim Holley
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, find me on LinkedIn. That's probably... Well, not probably, is my most professional platform. Instagram, like I said, is a farce. And being useful. Yeah, send me things that you're excited about in the Etsy product. Send me feedback. We're always really keen to learn how folks are experiencing the things that we build. Lenny (01:11:26) Amazing. Tim, thank you so much for being here. Tim Holley (01:11:28) Thank you for having me, Lenny. Appreciate it. Lenny (01:11:30) Bye everyone. (01:11:34) Thank you so much for listening. turns.zh:
是的，是的，可以在领英上找到我。这可能……嗯，不可能，是我最专业的平台。Instagram就像我说的，就是个闹剧。至于如何提供帮助……是的，欢迎把你在Etsy产品上感到兴奋的东西发给我。给我反馈。我们一直很想了解大家对我们开发的产品体验如何。  
莱尼（01:11:26）太棒了。蒂姆，非常感谢你能来。  
蒂姆·霍利（01:11:28）谢谢你邀请我，莱尼。  
莱尼（01:11:30）大家再见。（01:11:34）非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期内容有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅节目。也欢迎给我们评分或写评论，这对其他听众找到节目很有帮助。更多往期节目和节目信息，请访问lennyspodcast.com。下期节目见。
